Yugoslavia mobilised around 700,000 men in April 1941. The country stopped existing eleven days later.

The invasion of Yugoslavia, 1941, in four frames — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ It began with a signature. On 25 March 1941 Yugoslavia joined the Tripartite Pact. Two days later officers in Belgrade overthrew the regency, crowds filled the streets, and Hitler ordered the country destroyed — militarily and as a state.

2/ The attack opened on 6 April with the bombing of an undefended Belgrade. Four armies came in: German, Italian, Hungarian and Bulgarian. Panel one, 9 April: the red is already eating the edges, and Skopje in the south had fallen on day two.

3/ The defence had a geometry problem. Yugoslavia's border ran roughly 3,000 km and was hostile along almost all of it. There was no line to hold and no depth to fall back into — so the army was strung out everywhere and strong nowhere.

4/ It also had a loyalty problem. The kingdom was Serb-dominated and barely twenty years old. Croat and Slovene conscripts deserted in numbers, and on 10 April, as German troops entered Zagreb, the Ustaše proclaimed an Independent State of Croatia.

5/ Panels two and three, 12 and 14 April. Look at how fast the blue collapses inward. This is not a front line moving — it is a state dissolving, with units surrendering intact and communications gone within days.

6/ Panel four, 16 April. The surrender was signed the next day. King Peter II and the government were already out, en route to London via Greece. What followed was partition: annexations by Germany, Italy, Hungary, Bulgaria and Albania.

7/ The occupation was the opposite of the invasion. A country conquered in eleven days then tied down large Axis forces for four years and produced one of the largest resistance movements in occupied Europe.

8/ You'll often read that this campaign delayed Barbarossa and cost Hitler Moscow. Historians are divided — the spring thaw was late that year anyway. It's a tidy story, and tidy stories about weather and empires deserve suspicion.
